findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Before deleting the args file, save its 27 node ids. After the Windows run, check that each id appears with PASSED in the job log or test-report artifact (count == 27, zero SKIPPED). State the fallback (wait for the next scheduled run) if the dispatched run has no `sweep (windows)` job.
evidence: Testing ends at: 'get the `sweep (windows)` job id from `gh run view <run> --json jobs`' — no step inspects per-test outcomes
AC requires 'ran and passed (not skipped)' for 27 named tests; instrument is 'gh run view --job <id> --log'
Context: '27 tests in 5 modules, from the 5 scheduled runs'
VERIFY-COMMAND taxonomy (5): criterion names a count but no cardinality assertion is specified
findings.finding: The Windows verification procedure locates the `sweep (windows)` job but never says how to establish the AC's claim that all 27 previously deselected tests 'ran and passed (not skipped)'. A job concluding success does not prove this. A quiet pytest log (`-q`) does not list passing node ids, and a test could be skipped or deselected elsewhere. The procedure also assumes, without stating it, that a `workflow_dispatch` run actually includes the `sweep (windows)` job, although the evidence came from scheduled runs.
findings.location: Testing → Windows paragraph; AC '[non-codebase] On the Windows CI runner, the 27 tests ...'
scenarios: The sweep runs pytest with -q: the log shows only a summary line, so a reviewer can't tell whether the 27 specific ids passed or were skipped
The sweep job is gated to `schedule` events, so the dispatched run has no `sweep (windows)` job and the procedure dead-ends
findings.suggested_fix: Add to Testing: 'Before step 4, copy the 27 node ids to a scratch file. After the run, run `gh run view --job <id> --log > win.log` and, for each id, `grep -F "<id> PASSED" win.log`; require 27 matches and no SKIPPED for those ids. If the sweep does not print per-test results, add `-rA` to its pytest invocation or read the junit artifact instead. If the dispatched run has no `sweep (windows)` job, use the next scheduled run on a commit containing the fix.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In Approach step 1, name `tests/_subprocess_env.py::minimal_env` as existing prior art. Either state why the 19 callers can't adopt it (e.g. sentinel-first ordering, POSIX identity contract), or move the SYSTEMROOT key and lookup into `_subprocess_env` and use it from both helpers.
evidence: tests/_subprocess_env.py:40-50: `def minimal_env(...)`, docstring: 'Only ``SYSTEMROOT`` is carried from the ambient environment... Windows cannot load Winsock without it, so ``import asyncio`` in the child would fail with ``OSError: [WinError 10106]`` (bug arctic-unsecular-esok).'
minimal_env call sites: tests/unit/test_fs_tools_extraction.py:63, tests/unit/test_tracing.py:99, tests/unit/test_fixture_heal.py:321, tests/interfaces/store/test_llm_framework.py:36
The plan cites only product code as prior art: 'The same requirement is already handled in product code: src/rebar/grounding/terraform_corroborator.py:63'

Possible unstated reason for a separate helper: tests/unit/test_environ_assert_repr_security.py:134-135 says 'the sentinel leads, so pytest's bounded mapping repr cannot truncate it away'. minimal_env would put SYSTEMROOT first, while _child_env adds it last.
findings.finding: The plan builds a second SYSTEMROOT-forwarding mechanism in tests/_nested_pytest.py without mentioning the existing test helper `minimal_env()` in tests/_subprocess_env.py. That helper already forwards SYSTEMROOT for minimal child environments for the same WinError 10106 / asyncio Winsock failure. The plan neither reuses its logic nor explains why the 19 callers cannot use it, so two separate sources of truth for 'which OS-required key a minimal env must carry' can drift apart.
findings.location: Approach step 1 (tests/_nested_pytest.py `_child_env`); prior-art citation in Root causes item 1
scenarios: A later change to which OS keys a Windows child needs (e.g. adding WINDIR, as terraform_corroborator's _KEEP_ENV does) gets made in one helper and not the other.
A reviewer or maintainer can't tell which helper new minimal-env tests should use.
findings.suggested_fix: Add one sentence to Approach step 1: 'tests/_subprocess_env.py::minimal_env already forwards SYSTEMROOT for from-scratch envs; callers of run_nested_pytest are not switched to it because some (test_environ_assert_repr_security.py:134) need the sentinel first in the mapping and the POSIX contract requires the caller's object to pass through unchanged.' Optionally move the 'SYSTEMROOT' constant into tests/_subprocess_env.py and import it in _nested_pytest.py so both helpers share one definition.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the `_root_conftest` name match injectable (e.g. a `path_cls` defaulting to `Path`) and add POSIX unit cases. With `PureWindowsPath`, `r"D:\a\rebar\rebar\tests\conftest.py"` must match; with `PurePosixPath`, `xtests/conftest.py` must not.
evidence: '`Path` splits on the native separators (both `\` and `/` on Windows), so the same expression matches on both platforms'
Testing lists new cases only for `_child_env`; none for `_root_conftest`
Fallback: 'GitHub is a read-only mirror, so there is no pre-merge Windows run.'
findings.finding: Cause 2's fix (`Path(name).parts[-2:] == ("tests", "conftest.py")`) has no POSIX-runnable test of the Windows case. On POSIX, `Path` does not split backslashes, so `test_repo_isolation_guard.py` passing in `make verify` proves only that POSIX behavior is unchanged. Cause 1, by contrast, gets an injectable `os_name` and a simulated-Windows unit test. With no pre-merge Windows run, the backslash match is first exercised after merge. The claimed tightening (rejecting `xtests/conftest.py`) is also untested.
scenarios: A subtle mismatch, such as pytest registering the conftest under a different name form on Windows, is only discovered in the post-merge sweep and needs a follow-up change
findings.suggested_fix: Extract `_is_root_conftest_name(name, path_cls=Path) -> bool` returning `path_cls(name).parts[-2:] == ("tests", "conftest.py")`. Parametrize a test over (`PureWindowsPath`, backslash name, True), (`PurePosixPath`, '/r/tests/conftest.py', True) and (`PurePosixPath`, '/r/xtests/conftest.py', False).

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Widen the census to equality and key-set assertions on the env passed to `run_nested_pytest`/`subprocess.run`, and to child-side assertions on `os.environ` contents. Record its patterns and result in the plan.
evidence: 'A census of `tests/` for assertions on a captured `env` (`grep -rn '\["env"\] is'`) finds no other identity check on this helper's output.'
Approach step 1: 'The docstring contract "minimal mappings must not gain ambient keys" gains one stated exception'
findings.finding: The census meant to find tests broken by the new Windows exception searches only for identity checks (`grep -rn '\["env"\] is'`). It would miss equality assertions on the env passed to `subprocess.run` (e.g. `captured["env"] == {...}` or `kwargs["env"] ==`). It would also miss child-side tests that assert the child process environment contains only the minimal keys, which is the very contract ('minimal mappings must not gain ambient keys') being relaxed. Such tests would start failing on Windows once `SYSTEMROOT` is injected.
scenarios: A nested-pytest test asserts `set(os.environ) == {sentinel, guarded, 'PATH'}` inside the child. On Windows it now sees `SYSTEMROOT` and fails, which the post-merge sweep reports as a 'further cause'
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the census with e.g. `grep -rnE '\["env"\][[:space:]]*(is|==)|kwargs\["env"\]|set\(os\.environ\)|os\.environ\.keys\(\)' tests/`. Review each hit against the new Windows `SYSTEMROOT` exception.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the defaults: `_child_env(None)` returns `None` unchanged (the child inherits, and `SYSTEMROOT` is already present), and the copy is built as `type(env)({**env, "SYSTEMROOT": value})`, or via the named `SubprocessEnv` constructor.
evidence: 'if no key of the caller's mapping equals `SYSTEMROOT` case-insensitively ... it returns a copy with `SYSTEMROOT` added'
'The copy keeps the caller's mapping type (`SubprocessEnv` stays `SubprocessEnv` ...)'
findings.finding: `_child_env` is defined by scanning the caller mapping's keys. The plan does not say what happens when `env` is `None` (inherit the parent environment) or is not a dict-like mapping. It also does not say how the type-preserving copy is built for `SubprocessEnv`, for example whether its constructor accepts a mapping.
scenarios: A caller passes `env=None` and `_child_env` raises on key iteration on Windows

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Widen the caller census beyond identity checks: grep the 19 tests and their child-script bodies for equality or key-set assertions on the env or `os.environ` (e.g. `== {`, `set(os.environ`, `len(os.environ`), and record the result or adjust those tests to tolerate the Windows-only SYSTEMROOT.
evidence: "A census of `tests/` for assertions on a captured `env` (`grep -rn '\["env"\] is'`) finds no other identity check on this helper's output."
"The docstring contract 'minimal mappings must not gain ambient keys' gains one stated exception"

The 19 tests are secret-redaction tests that build hand-made minimal envs (e.g. `{sentinel, guarded var, "PATH"}` at test_environ_assert_repr_security.py:136). Exact env contents are plausibly what some of them assert.
findings.finding: The census of callers that depend on the old exact-environment behavior is too narrow. It only greps for identity checks (`["env"] is`). On Windows the child now receives an extra SYSTEMROOT key, so any equality or key-set assertion could break. Such assertions could live in the parent test or inside the child scripts launched by the 19 secret-redaction tests (for example, a child that asserts its os.environ holds only the sentinel, the guarded var and PATH). They would fail for a third cause that the plan has not surveyed.
findings.location: Approach step 2 — 'A census of `tests/` for assertions on a captured `env` (`grep -rn '\["env"\] is'`) finds no other identity check'
scenarios: The post-merge Windows sweep runs a test whose child asserts `sorted(os.environ) == [...]` or `len(os.environ) == 3`. The extra SYSTEMROOT key makes it fail, and the fallback path must re-deselect it.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State that `_child_env` returns `env` unchanged when it is None (inherit), or that run_nested_pytest never accepts None, and add an nt-mode unit case for that input.
evidence: "On `os_name == \"nt\"`, if no key of the caller's mapping equals `SYSTEMROOT` case-insensitively ... it returns a copy with `SYSTEMROOT` added. In every other case it returns the caller's object itself"
The Testing cases cover only mapping inputs; there is no None / inherit case.
findings.finding: The `_child_env` spec does not define its behavior when `env` is None or another non-mapping value. If `run_nested_pytest` accepts `env=None` (meaning 'inherit the parent environment'), the nt branch is undefined: 'no key of the caller's mapping equals SYSTEMROOT' cannot be evaluated on None. A naive implementation would either raise TypeError or replace inheritance with a one-key `{SYSTEMROOT: ...}` environment. Neither case is covered by the listed unit tests.
findings.location: Approach step 1 — `_child_env(env, *, os_name=os.name, ambient=os.environ)`; Testing — new cases in tests/unit/test_nested_pytest_helper.py
scenarios: A current or future caller of run_nested_pytest omits env (None) on Windows. `_child_env` either crashes iterating None, or builds `{"SYSTEMROOT": ...}` and strips PATH and everything else from the child, so the child cannot even find its interpreter's dependencies.
findings.suggested_fix: In `_child_env`, return `env` unchanged when `env is None`, before applying the nt/SYSTEMROOT logic, and add `assert _child_env(None, os_name="nt", ambient={"SYSTEMROOT": "C:\\Windows"}) is None` to the new unit tests (only if run_nested_pytest's signature permits None).

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Build the census of tests affected by the change to `run_nested_pytest` env from `find_referencing_symbols` on `run_nested_pytest` and `_child_env`, plus a string grep for `run_nested_pytest`, `monkeypatch.setattr(subprocess, "run"` and other env-capture spellings (`kwargs["env"]`, `kwargs.get("env")`, `os.environ` key-set assertions in probe bodies). Record the result instead of the single `'\["env"\] is'` grep.
evidence: Plan text: "A census of `tests/` for assertions on a captured `env` (`grep -rn '\["env"\] is'`) finds no other identity check on this helper's output." The plan names its own method: a grep for one spelling.

run_nested_pytest has about 25 callers, e.g. tests/unit/test_crash_guard.py:41/90/112/191/260, tests/unit/test_timeout_budget.py:95-282, tests/unit/test_engine_dir.py:184/239, tests/scripts/test_autodeploy_env_repr_security.py:24. None of them was listed or checked by symbol lookup.

Other capture spellings exist in the repo and the plan's pattern would miss them, e.g. tests/unit/test_spawn_detached.py:121 (`captured.kwargs["env"]`) and tests/unit/reconciler/orchestrate/test_orchestrator_wiring.py:420 (`kwargs.get("env")`).
findings.finding: The plan builds the inventory of tests affected by the change to `run_nested_pytest` with a single grep pattern rather than from a lookup of the helper's references. On Windows the helper now passes a copy of `env` instead of the caller's object. The plan's census of tests that assert on that env was produced by `grep -rn '\["env"\] is'`. That pattern only catches the identity spelling `["env"] is`. It misses `captured.kwargs["env"]`, `kwargs.get("env")`, equality or key-set checks, and probe children that inspect `os.environ`. I found no omitted site, but that is luck, not proof.
findings.location: Approach step 2: "A census of `tests/` for assertions on a captured `env` (`grep -rn '\["env"\] is'`) finds no other identity check on this helper's output."
scenarios: A caller of run_nested_pytest that patches subprocess.run and records `kwargs.get("env")` or `captured.kwargs["env"]`, then checks identity or exact equality against its minimal mapping, would start failing on the Windows sweep. The grep census would not have found it.

A probe child launched through run_nested_pytest that asserts an exact `os.environ` key set would see an extra `SYSTEMROOT` on Windows and fail after the deselect file is removed. Neither the grep nor the plan's Scope would have caught it.
findings.suggested_fix: In Approach step 2, replace the grep-based census sentence with: run `find_referencing_symbols` on `run_nested_pytest` to list every caller, and separately grep tests/ for the string `run_nested_pytest` and for env-capture spellings (`["env"]`, `kwargs.get("env")`, `set(os.environ)`). State that only tests/unit/test_nested_pytest_helper.py patches subprocess.run around the helper, and that no probe child asserts an exact environment key set.
